query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation followed by a controlled partial annealing treatment will induce a nanostructured microstructure in equiatomic FeCoNi high‐entropy alloys, enhancing domain‐wall pinning and thus increasing coercivity relative to earlier, undeformed FeCoNiPd/FeCoNiPt soft ferromagnetic derivatives.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with an fcc structure exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., cold-rolling or high-pressure torsion) at ambient or moderately elevated temperatures, followed by partial annealing at approximately 500–600 °C.
generation.conditions: Maintain near-equiatomic composition with a configurational entropy ≥1.0R; process the alloy under controlled severe deformation and partial recovery conditions to avoid full recrystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanometer-sized grains and a high density of lattice defects (e.g., dislocations), which serve as domain-wall pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: The introduced nanoscale grain refinement and controlled defect structures act to impede magnetic domain-wall motion, thereby raising the coercivity while retaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.predicted_outcome: An observable increase in coercivity (i.e., a shift toward magnetically harder behavior) when compared to the baseline undeformed FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys such as FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt.
generation.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys (e.g., FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt) that display soft ferromagnetism with low coercivity.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected when the deformation conditions produce controlled nanostructure refinement without inducing a full recrystallization; significant deviations in deformation strain, temperature, or annealing time may negate the domain-wall pinning benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the coercivity enhancement is uncertain and may depend sensitively on the exact processing parameters and microstructural evolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy samples under identical compositional conditions. Process one set with severe plastic deformation (via cold-rolling or high-pressure torsion) followed by partial annealing at 500–600 °C, while keeping the other set as an undeformed control (or fully recrystallized reference). Characterize both sets using microscopy (TEM/SEM) to confirm nanostructure and defect density, and measure their magnetic properties (coercivity and saturation magnetization) via vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) under similar conditions.
measurements: Grain size and defect density (via TEM/SEM)
Magnetic hysteresis loops (via VSM) to extract coercivity values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the processed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercivity (e.g., >20% relative improvement) compared to the undeformed or fully recrystallized FeCoNi baseline while maintaining comparable saturation magnetization.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. The physical metallurgy of superalloys [9] have been employed to design HEAs by utilization of significant volume fractions of stable and coherent L1 2 γ′ to provide high temperature strength, e.g., Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 HEA was designed to contain 46 vol% of γ′ precipitates [10] , and its tensile strength could surpass those of Inconel 617 and All

For centuries, constructions with high mechanical requirements have been built using steel or iron-based alloys, while titanium or aluminum have been used for light-weight constructions. In gas turbines nickel- or cobalt-based superalloys are used because of their extremely good mechanical properties and oxidation resistance over long periods of time at high temperatures. The main properties of these alloys are given by their base element, while the addition of other elements in small amounts leads to fine adjustments of a specific behavior [ [1] ].

An unconventional approach of alloy design is based not on a main element, but on a chemical composition that exhibits a large number of elements with none of them dominating. In this group one differentiates between single-phase high entropy alloys (HEA) [ [2] ] and multiphase compositionally complex alloys (CCA). Multicomponent alloys were examined first by Yeh [ [2] ] and Cantor [ [3] ]. Investigating the microstructure of alloys with different numbers of elements in equiatomic mixtures, Cantor found the five-component, equiatomic alloy Co 20 Cr 20 Fe 20 Mn 20 Ni 20 to form a single-phase solid-solution. decision.trend: No prior work in the provided references directly investigates the coercivity of FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys or attempts to harden their soft ferromagnetism. Although some papers (e.g., PMC4999872, PMC5461481) involve fcc CoCrFe(Ni)-type alloys and explore phase stability, irradiation, and polymorphic transitions, none address the challenge of increasing coercivity in FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys. Thus, the specific question of enhancing coercivity in an equiatomic (≥1.0R configurational entropy) FeCoNi system remains open in these references.
decision.unsolved: Despite high saturation magnetization and equiatomic compositions, FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys so far remain ‘soft’ ferromagnets (low coercivity). A clear strategy to establish magnetically hard phases or domain-wall pinning features—without simply altering chemistry via new element additions—has not been demonstrated in the referenced literature.
decision.lever: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., cold-rolling or high-pressure torsion) at ambient or moderately elevated temperature, followed by partial annealing (∼500–600 °C) to create nanoscale grain refinement and controlled lattice defects that pin domain walls, increasing coercivity.
decision.why: By restricting composition changes (to maintain near-equiatomic FeCoNi with ≥1.0R entropy) and leveraging known fcc microstructural tunability via deformation and recovery, one can introduce high dislocation densities, refined grains, or short-range ordered clusters. These features will impede magnetic domain-wall motion and raise coercivity while preserving high saturation magnetization. Prior studies of FeCoNi-based alloys (e.g., CoCrFeNi systems under plastic deformation and thermal treatment) indicate robust microstructure control is achievable and strongly impacts mechanical and structural properties, suggesting a parallel effect on magnetic hardness is plausible. Experimentally, systematically varying deformation strain and partial annealing temperature/time, then measuring the resulting coercivity will test the hypothesis. Falsification occurs if a refined microstructure does not produce detectably higher coercivity than in the undeformed or fully recrystallized FeCoNi-based baseline.
